record.paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
record.context_brief: Atmospheric neutrinos as a proton-spectrum test
record.original_question: Can atmospheric-neutrino measurements above about 100 TeV distinguish between competing parent cosmic-ray proton spectra inferred by experiments such as ARGO-YBJ and KASCADE, despite the onset of an astrophysical neutrino component whose origin and experimental uncertainties are not yet understood well enough to draw clear conclusions?

evidence.quote: Important information could be deduced, in principle, by the measurement of the flux of atmospheric neutrinos, sensitive to the spectrum of parent CRs. In particular, the tail of the spectrum of atmospheric neutrinos is mainly shaped by the parent protons rather than by heavier element.

As a consequence, we expect different predictions for the flux of atmospheric neutrinos according to ARGO-YBJ and KASCADE proton energy spectra, predictions that, in principle, can be checked at energies Eν ≥ 100 TeV if the atmospheric neutrinos could be properly identified.

Unfortunately, in this energy region the total neutrino flux detected by IceCube departs from the existing predictions for atmospheric neutrinos suggesting the onset of an astrophysical component. The origin of such neutrinos is still unknown and current experimental uncertainties do not allow to draw clear conclusions [71].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Cosmic-ray (CR) measurements have produced competing determinations of the energy spectrum of primary protons in the energy region around the "knee" (roughly 10^14–10^16 eV). Two notable determinations are those reported by the ARGO-YBJ experiment and by the KASCADE experiment, which differ both in spectral index and in absolute normalization in this range.

Atmospheric neutrinos are produced by the decay of mesons created when primary cosmic rays interact in the Earth's atmosphere. At high neutrino energies, the high-energy tail of the atmospheric neutrino spectrum is dominated by contributions from parent protons (rather than from heavier nuclei), so different assumed primary-proton spectra translate into measurably different predicted atmospheric neutrino fluxes, in particular for neutrino energies E_ν ≳ 100 TeV.

At these energies, however, the measured neutrino flux contains, in addition to the atmospheric component, a diffuse astrophysical neutrino component of presently unknown origin, with experimental uncertainties on flavor composition, spectral shape and normalization.

Question: Determine whether current and near-future measurements of the atmospheric neutrino flux at energies E_ν ≥ 100 TeV can, in principle and in practice, discriminate between the parent-proton primary cosmic-ray spectra inferred respectively by ARGO-YBJ and by KASCADE. Specifically, identify under what assumptions about the separation of the atmospheric and astrophysical neutrino components (including conventional and prompt contributions) the two proton-spectrum hypotheses produce statistically distinguishable predictions for the observable high-energy atmospheric neutrino flux.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent IceCube analyses (through 2024–2025) continue to refine the atmospheric and astrophysical neutrino flux separation above 100 TeV, but uncertainties on the prompt atmospheric component and on the diffuse astrophysical flux remain large enough that no published analysis claims a definitive discrimination between ARGO-YBJ- and KASCADE-inferred proton spectra using ≥100 TeV atmospheric neutrinos. The discrimination remains a stated prospect rather than an achieved result.

status_evidence.title: Characterization of the Astrophysical Diffuse Neutrino Flux using Starting Track Events in IceCube
status_evidence.snippet: IceCube measures the astrophysical diffuse flux at 100 TeV with a per-flavor normalization of 1.68 ×10⁻¹⁸ GeV⁻¹ cm⁻² s⁻¹ sr⁻¹.
status_evidence.claim: Astrophysical diffuse flux above 100 TeV is measured but with sizable uncertainties affecting separation from atmospheric component.

status_evidence.title: Constraining the Prompt Atmospheric Neutrino Flux Combining IceCube's Cascade and Track Samples
status_evidence.snippet: Constraining the Prompt Atmospheric Neutrino Flux Combining IceCube's Cascade and Track Samples
status_evidence.claim: The prompt atmospheric neutrino component is still being constrained, indicating the atmospheric high-energy tail is not yet pinned down.

status_evidence.title: Measurement of the atmospheric neutrino energy spectrum from 100 GeV to 400 TeV with IceCube
status_evidence.snippet: Measurement of the atmospheric neutrino energy spectrum from 100 GeV to 400 TeV with IceCube
status_evidence.claim: Atmospheric neutrino energy spectrum has been measured up to ~400 TeV, providing the basic data needed but not yet sufficient to distinguish ARGO-YBJ vs KASCADE proton spectra.
